**Problem.** Determine all automorphisms of the field $F(x)$ that fix $F$, by describing their values on $x$.

**Answer.** The $F$-automorphisms of $F(x)$ are exactly the fractional linear (Möbius) transformations
$$\sigma(x) = \frac{ax+b}{cx+d}, \qquad a,b,c,d \in F,\quad ad-bc \neq 0.$$

---

**Proof.**

Let $\sigma$ be an $F$-automorphism of $F(x)$. Write
$$\sigma(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, \qquad p,q \in F[x],\ \gcd(p,q)=1,\ q\neq 0.$$
Set $y = \sigma(x) = p(x)/q(x)$. Since $\sigma$ fixes $F$, every element of $F(x)$ is sent to the corresponding rational function evaluated at $y$, so $\sigma(F(x)) = F(y) \subseteq F(x)$. The map $\sigma$ is an automorphism iff it is surjective, i.e. iff $F(y)=F(x)$, i.e. iff $[F(x):F(y)]=1$.

**Key claim.** $[F(x):F(y)] = \max(\deg p,\, \deg q)$.

*Proof of claim.* The element $x$ satisfies
$$p(T) - y\,q(T) = 0 \quad\text{evaluated at } T=x,$$
i.e. $x$ is a root of $f(T) := p(T)-y\,q(T) \in F(y)[T]$, which has degree $n:=\max(\deg p,\deg q)$ in $T$ (the leading terms of $p$ and $q$ cannot both cancel, since $\gcd(p,q)=1$ forces them to have distinct leading monomials unless one is constant; in any case $\deg_T f = n$).

We show $f$ is irreducible in $F(y)[T]$. View $f = p(T)-y\,q(T)$ as a polynomial in $F[T][y]$; it is *linear* in $y$. Hence any factorization in $F[T][y]$ must have one factor of $y$-degree $0$, i.e. lying in $F[T]$. Such a factor would divide both $p(T)$ and $q(T)$, hence (by $\gcd(p,q)=1$) is a unit in $F[T]$. So $f$ is irreducible in $F[T][y]=F[y][T]$. As a polynomial in $T$ over $F[y]$, it is primitive (its $y$-coefficients $p(T),-q(T)$ are coprime in $F[T]$). By Gauss's Lemma, $f$ remains irreducible in $F(y)[T]$.

Therefore $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $x$ over $F(y)$, giving $[F(x):F(y)]=n$. $\square$

**Conclusion of necessity.** $\sigma$ is an automorphism iff $[F(x):F(y)]=1$ iff $n=\max(\deg p,\deg q)=1$. Thus
$$\sigma(x)=\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$$
with $a,b,c,d\in F$. The condition $\gcd(p,q)=1$ together with $\deg p,\deg q\le 1$ means the two linear (or constant) polynomials $ax+b$ and $cx+d$ are not proportional, i.e. $ad-bc\neq 0$ (if $ad-bc=0$, then $(a,b)$ is proportional to $(c,d)$ and the ratio is constant, contradicting surjectivity).

**Sufficiency.** Conversely, given $a,b,c,d\in F$ with $ad-bc\neq 0$, define $\sigma(x)=(ax+b)/(cx+d)$. The inverse transformation is
$$\sigma^{-1}(x)=\frac{dx-b}{-cx+a},$$
which is again of the same form with determinant $da-(-c)b=ad-bc\neq 0$. Hence $\sigma$ is an invertible $F$-endomorphism of $F(x)$, i.e. an $F$-automorphism.

**Composition structure.** These transformations compose as
$$\frac{a_2\!\left(\frac{a_1 x+b_1}{c_1 x+d_1}\right)+b_2}{c_2\!\left(\frac{a_1 x+b_1}{c_1 x+d_1}\right)+d_2} = \frac{(a_2 a_1+b_2 c_1)x+(a_2 b_1+b_2 d_1)}{(c_2 a_1+d_2 c_1)x+(c_2 b_1+d_2 d_1)},$$
i.e. via matrix multiplication $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. The condition $ad-bc\neq 0$ identifies these matrices with $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$, and scalar matrices $\lambda I$ act trivially, so the automorphism group is
$$\mathrm{Aut}_F(F(x)) \cong \mathrm{PGL}_2(F).$$

---

**Summary.** The $F$-automorphisms of $F(x)$ are precisely the maps
$$\boxed{\,\sigma(x)=\dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d},\quad a,b,c,d\in F,\ ad-bc\neq 0\,}$$
forming a group isomorphic to $\mathrm{PGL}_2(F)$ under composition.

### PROOF COMPLETE
